title: What Makes Infrastructure Intelligent? Start with the Network
summary: Every network packet tells a story. NETSCOUT Smart Data helps intelligent infrastructure understand what is happening by analyzing network interactions. So stop skimming the chapters.
body_markdown:
Infrastructure is “learning” to pay attention. Literally and figuratively. Devices send data to applications. Systems call other systems. Every exchange on the network leaves evidence of how the larger environment is working. The story starts to make sense when you read those interactions together.


The[World Economic Forum](https://www.weforum.org/stories/manufacturing-and-value-chains/what-is-intelligent-infrastructure-and-how-is-it-redefining-industrial-competitiveness/) describes intelligent infrastructure as a digital backbone that brings sensors and connectivity together with data platforms. This may include smart devices and Internet of Things (IoT) systems along with industrial controls, analytics, AI, and automation.


It’s simple: Digital infrastructure connects; intelligent infrastructure understands and acts. This matters wherever physical operations depend on digital services.


On a[modern manufacturing floor](https://www.netscout.com/industries/manufacturing) , for example, business applications and[cloud services](https://www.netscout.com/solutions/cloud-observability) work alongside specialized machinery and connected equipment. At an[airport](https://www.netscout.com/industries/transportation/airports) , passenger processing and baggage handling depend on flight information moving between airline and airport systems. When something changes in either environment, IT and operations teams need to figure out what else may be involved.


## Intelligence Starts with Understanding Change in Context


Connected environments are constantly collecting and processing data. A service’s behavior may shift as devices or systems join the network and users log on or off.


The real question, then, is this: What else was affected as conditions changed, such as during an application slowdown or a software update? That means knowing which systems are talking to each other and how those interactions relate to the services people or machines are using.


Context is everything. It comes from piecing together how events unfolded across systems, even when the sequence is not as simple as A + B = C.


A blind spot, for example, may hide an important connection or make an ordinary fluctuation, such as a brief traffic spike during a scheduled backup, initially look more important than it is. AI can help by evaluating those relationships much faster than a person moving among separate tools, but its conclusions still depend on the quality of the operational data available to it. Packets show how services and devices are interacting in real time and how they interacted historically, so teams or autonomous systems have concrete evidence to work from.


## What Intelligent Infrastructure Needs


Technology changes from one environment to another, but the operational challenge is familiar. Information has to move reliably, and teams have to understand how one system affects another to help reduce alert fatigue and avoid costly disruptions. Several capabilities make that possible:


- **Continuous awareness:** Important activity may occur in a data center or cloud environment. It can also originate at a[remote facility](https://www.netscout.com/solutions/remote-site-observability) or on the network edge. Teams need access to real-time data wherever services operate.
- **Relationship awareness:** Applications, devices, and infrastructure components are part of a larger ecosystem. Seeing how they communicate and depend on each other helps reveal what may be affected when behavior changes.
- **Adaptability:** Data from across the environment should help organizations respond as conditions shift. It should also show whether an adjustment, such as a virtual private network configuration change, worked.
- **Clear evidence:** AI, analytics, and automation need millisecond-level, packet-derived context to distinguish ordinary fluctuations from issues requiring action. Without it, normal activity can trigger an unnecessary response, while early warning signs may go unnoticed.


For instance, in a connected building, HVAC controls and elevators may share digital infrastructure with security technology and workplace applications. When one system behaves differently, facilities and IT teams have to determine whether the change is isolated or part of something larger. Seeing those[interactions on the network](https://www.netscout.com/solutions/network-observability) helps them understand the building as one operating environment.
